'''''Erythronium oregonum''''' is a [[North America]]n species of flowering plant in the [[Liliaceae|lily family]] which is known by the common name '''giant white fawnlily''' or '''Oregon fawn-lily'''.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Erythronium oregonum in Flora of North America @ efloras.org |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242101599 |access-date=2022-09-29 |website=www.efloras.org}}</ref><ref name="calflora.org">{{Cite web |title=Erythronium oregonum Calflora |url=https://www.calflora.org/app/taxon?crn=3505 |access-date=2022-09-29 |website=www.calflora.org}}</ref>
[[File:Erythronium oregonum.jpg|thumb|''Erythronium oregonum flower'']]
It is native to western [[North America]], where it grows in the [[Pacific Coast Ranges]] from southwestern [[British Columbia]] to northern [[California]].<ref name=sarahmanning/><ref>[https://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Erythronium%20oregonum.png Biota of North America Program 2014 county distribution map]</ref><ref name="calflora.org"/>

== Distribution and habitat ==
In [[North America]] from southern [[British Columbia]] south to northern [[California]], west of the [[Cascade Range]] to the Coast Range and [[Siskiyou Mountains|Siskiyous]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pnwflowers.com/flower/erythronium-oregonum|title=Erythronium oregonum {{!}} Oregon fawn lily {{!}} Wildflowers of the Pacific Northwest|website=www.pnwflowers.com|access-date=2018-04-01}}</ref> It grows in meadows, rocky outcrops, and coniferous forests.<ref name=":1" />

==Description==
''Erythronium oregonum'' is wildflower growing from a [[bulb]] 3 to 5 centimeters wide and produces basal, lance-shaped green leaves up to 22 centimeters long and often mottled with brown and white. Thin naked stalks reach up to about 40 centimeters in height, each bearing one flower or sometimes more.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Fagan|first=Damian|title=Wildflowers of Oregon: A Field Guide to Over 400 Wildflowers, Trees, and Shrubs of the Coast, Cascades, and High Desert|publisher=[[FalconGuides]]|year=2019|isbn=978-1-4930-3633-2|location=Guilford, CT|pages=56|oclc=1073035766}}</ref>

Each flower has white [[tepal]]s with yellow bases, sometimes streaked with dull red. The flower is often nodding, facing the ground. Its tepals are recurved so their points face upward. The [[stamen]]s and [[Gynoecium|stigma]] are white and the anthers may be white to yellow. They are pollinated by beetles and flies.<ref name=":0" />

== Uses ==
Bears have been known to eat the entire plant.<ref name=":0" />

Native Americans ate the roots raw or cooked.<ref name=":0" />{{Specify |reason=Which groups of Native Americans? When? Why past tense?|date=August 2023}}

== History ==
"[[John Burroughs]] is said to have named this species 'fawn lily' because he thought the two leaves looked like the pricked ears of a fawn. More likely, 'fawn' alludes to the mottled leaf coloring."<ref>{{Cite book|title=Plants of the Pacific Northwest Coast|last=Pojar, Mackinnon|first=Jim, Andy|publisher=Lone Pine Publishing|year=1994|isbn=1-55105-040-4|location=Vancouver, BC|pages=104}}</ref>
